title: BamSEC in 2026: Pricing and What to Use Instead
summary: What BamSEC costs in 2026, what the AlphaSense acquisition actually changed, what it still does better than anyone, and where analysts hit its limits.
body_markdown:
BamSEC has been the default answer to "how do I read SEC filings without fighting EDGAR" for over a decade. Two things have changed since most of the reviews you will find were written: it is no longer an independent company, and the job analysts need done has moved past navigation.


This is a straight look at what BamSEC costs today, what its acquisition actually changed, what it still does better than anyone, and where you will hit its edges.


We build Hudson Labs, which competes with BamSEC on part of its territory, so weigh the scoring accordingly. There is a full section below on what BamSEC does better than us. If you want the head-to-head rather than the review, we have a separate[Hudson Labs vs. BamSEC comparison](https://www.hudson-labs.com/blog/hudson-labs-vs-bamsec) .


## What BamSEC is


BamSEC is SEC filing navigation software. It takes EDGAR, which is free but hostile, and turns it into something readable: categorized filing views, key exhibits pulled out and organized, earnings transcripts, tables you can push to Excel, keyword and Boolean search across documents, and email alerts when a watchlist company files.


It gained traction with institutional investors because it is fast and because the interface gets out of the way. That reputation is deserved. BamSEC remains a benchmark for user-centric design in financial software.


What it does not do is analyse. It puts the document in front of you cleanly and leaves the reading to you. For a long time that was the whole job.

A few things worth knowing before you buy:


The $69 figure is the annual rate. BamSEC does not advertise a month-to-month option on the public plan, so the practical commitment is $828 up front.


The pricing page no longer states a trial length. Third-party review sites report seven days, but we would confirm that at signup rather than trust a number you read somewhere.


Enterprise sales and trials are handled through AlphaSense.


## What BamSEC does well


**Navigation speed.** If your day is "open the 10-K, jump to the debt footnote, read it," BamSEC gets you there in fewer clicks than anything else on the market. It has held that position for a decade.


**Exhibit organization.** Credit agreements, indentures, press releases and 8-K exhibits are easier to browse in BamSEC than in platforms costing ten times more.


**Price.** $69/month is inexpensive for a tool an analyst opens every day, and the free tier is a reasonable way to try it.


**No AI to second-guess.** Some work requires that a person read the primary document, full stop. Compliance-sensitive research, litigation support, anything where a wrong number is a career event. A tool with no generative layer is the safer purchase for that constraint, and BamSEC is exactly that.


**Nothing to learn.** You will be productive in five minutes. That matters more than it sounds like it should.


## Where BamSEC stops


The limits are all the same limit, viewed from different angles: BamSEC is built to serve you one document at a time.


**Cross-company questions.** "Which US industrials extended their depreciation useful lives in the last two years, and what did it do to operating income?" is not a keyword search. It is a semantic question across thousands of filings. In BamSEC that is a multi-week research project.


**Restated figures.** Pulling a number is easy. Pulling a comparable multi-year series when the company has restated twice is not, and it is where most manual extraction quietly goes wrong.


**Language drift.** Which risk factors were added, removed or softened between filings. How guidance phrasing moved quarter over quarter. You can find this by hand if you know where to look and have the time.


**Alerting on findings.** BamSEC tells you a filing arrived. It cannot tell you the CFO departed and no accounting disagreement was disclosed.


None of these are defects. They are the boundary of the product BamSEC chose to build.


## Does BamSEC have AI?


Not in the sense people usually mean. BamSEC's product is navigation, search and table tools rather than generative analysis, and its marketing does not claim otherwise. The AI capabilities in that corporate family sit in AlphaSense, at AlphaSense pricing.


If you want AI over filings at self-serve prices, BamSEC is not the tool, and the AlphaSense upsell is a different budget conversation.


## Who should still buy BamSEC


**Individual investors and retail.** The free tier or Pro. An analysis layer is overkill unless you run a concentrated book.


**Anyone whose bottleneck is finding documents.** Buy it and stop reading reviews.


**Compliance-sensitive workflows.** Where a generative layer is a liability rather than a feature.


**Existing AlphaSense customers.** It is already adjacent to your stack. Price the AlphaSense seat against alternatives at renewal, but consolidation is a fair reason to stay.


## What to use instead


If your bottleneck has moved from finding to reading, these are the credible options.


**Hudson Labs.** Ours. Core is $119/month, or $99/month billed annually, with a 14-day trial. It covers the same filing navigation and table extraction ground, then adds cited extraction with a link back to the source line, restatement-adjusted figures across five years or twenty quarters, guidance and sentiment tracking, and AI screening across more than **10,000** companies. The Institutional plan adds forensic accounting red flags and securities class action risk scoring. Everything AI-extracted carries a No Hallucination Guarantee, which exists because "the model said so" does not belong in an investment memo.


**AlphaSense.** The parent company. Much broader content, including broker research and expert call transcripts, at enterprise pricing.


**Fintool and Fiscal.ai.** AI-native and conversational, lighter on forensic depth.


**Hebbia.** Document intelligence, strong on internal documents, not filings-specific.


**CapEdge.** Free, reasonable filings and transcript coverage, no analysis layer.


**FactSet and S&P Capital IQ.** Full data terminals. A different budget solving a different problem.


**SEC EDGAR full-text search.** Free, and better than people assume for simple lookups.

## A worked example


Take one question and run it both ways.


*Has this company been extending the useful life of its assets to flatter earnings?*


In BamSEC: open the current 10-K, find the significant accounting policies note, read the useful-life ranges. Open the prior-year 10-K, find the same note, compare by eye. Repeat for three more years. Then find depreciation expense in each year, work out what the change was worth, and check whether management quantified it anywhere. Twenty to forty minutes per company if you know exactly where to look, and BamSEC's navigation is what keeps it at twenty rather than sixty.


In Hudson Labs: ask for the useful-life assumption by year, the direction of each change, the dollar effect on operating income and the verbatim filing language. A cited table comes back. Then run the same question as a screen across the sector to find every other company that did it.


That is the real shape of the gap. BamSEC makes the manual version fast. An analysis layer removes the manual version, which changes which questions you are willing to ask at all.


## Frequently asked questions


**Is BamSEC still available after the AlphaSense acquisition?**


Yes. BamSEC became part of AlphaSense in July 2024, when AlphaSense acquired Tegus, which had acquired BamSEC in 2021. AlphaSense has said BamSEC continues to operate as a standalone product for self-serve SEC filing and transcript research.


**How much does BamSEC cost?**


BamSEC Pro is $69 per month billed annually, which works out to $828 per year. There is a limited free tier and a free trial on the paid plan. Enterprise pricing is custom and is handled through AlphaSense.


**Does BamSEC have a free version?**


Yes, with limited access. SEC EDGAR full-text search and CapEdge are also free. None of the free options include an analysis layer.


**Does BamSEC have AI?**


BamSEC's product is filing navigation, search and table tools rather than generative AI analysis. The AI capabilities in that family of products sit in AlphaSense.


**Is BamSEC worth it in 2026?**


If your bottleneck is finding and reading individual filings, yes. $69 per month is inexpensive for a tool used daily. If your bottleneck is answering questions across many companies at once, you will outgrow it.


**What is the best BamSEC alternative?**


It depends on the bottleneck. For AI analysis over filings, Hudson Labs. For breadth of content, AlphaSense. For a free option, EDGAR full-text search or CapEdge.


**Can I use BamSEC and an AI research tool together?**


Yes, and many analysts do. BamSEC and Hudson Labs Core together run about $170 per month and cover different halves of the workflow.


## The bottom line


BamSEC solves a 2015 problem better than anyone still solves it, at a fair price, and it is not going anywhere. If navigation is what slows you down, buy it.


The reason to look elsewhere is not that BamSEC got worse. It is that the work changed. Reading one filing carefully is table stakes now. The questions that move a thesis are the ones that span forty companies and five years of footnotes, and no navigation tool is going to answer those.


A test worth running: look at the last three research questions you dropped because they would have taken too long. If they were "where is that document," BamSEC is your answer. If they were "how many companies did X," you need something that reads.
